Steve Ballmer recalls that in Microsoft, they got rid of the value called teamwork, preferring open, respectful, and dedicated to making others better, because teamwork could sound like a treat.

thesis: This episode argues that Microsoft's historical success was built on a one-time fee licensing model that defined modern software, contrasting with Google's advertising-based approach which allowed it to dominate the mobile market. The speaker suggests Microsoft missed the mobile opportunity due to being locked into its legacy model, while Ballmer personally holds Microsoft stock for emotional reasons and to fund philanthropy without selling.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Microsoft's early history, noting that they paid around $45,000 to $49,000 for an operating system and later sold it for a significant profit, calling it a 'pretty good deal'.
claims.quote: I think we paid $45,000 or $49,000 for this operating system, because we told IBM no, no. We can take care of it. There was a famous meeting amongst me, Paul, Bill, and this guy Kazuhiko Nishi, who ran our affiliate in Japan, where we were talking about this.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Microsoft sold the operating system for a fraction of the cost, saying 'Twenty times $21,000, $400,000 against $50,000 we paid for it. Pretty good deal.'
claims.quote: We said, we can do this 10–20 times. Twenty times $21,000, $400,000 against $50,000 we paid for it. Pretty good deal. It was a little better than that as you said.

claims.claim: The speaker explains that Microsoft did not charge for the operating system on an ongoing basis initially, but rather charged a one-time fee, and later switched to licensing per unit.
claims.quote: Remember, the key thing was we didn't charge for the operating system on an ongoing basis. We charged for it one time. If you got a new version, we charged another time. We did the same thing for BASIC and everything else, because at the time you could think we were like a substitute for an R&D department, which means we were fixed price.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that Microsoft defined what a modern software business looked like, with the notion that there could be lots of developers, and that there was no licensing model or business model at the time.
claims.quote: Really, I would say we—few other companies, but I would say we—defined what a modern software business looked like. The notion that there could be lots of developers and yeah, there were some, but it's not like we think today. There were developers doing lots of standard applications. No. There was no licensing model, no business model. Nothing.

claims.claim: The speaker mentions that Microsoft was not an enterprise company well into the 90s, and that they had to hang on to IBM, calling them the bear.
claims.quote: We weren't an enterprise company. If you looked at the enterprise, the enterprise was still… David: IBM. Steve: IBM. We used to say we had to hang on to IBM, that if we ever let go they might trample us. We called them the bear.

claims.claim: The speaker describes how Microsoft kept going with Windows and OS/2, and that Windows was their plan, while IBM wanted to do a new operating system.
claims.quote: We kept going with Windows, we kept going with OS/2, and then May 1990, they come along and shoot us. I was out running with my wife. I stopped. David: Wait, IBM shot you? Steve: Yeah, they divorced us. They threw us out.

claims.quote: I'd shipped when I'd been the development manager for Windows 1.0. David: Oh, the great videos of you from the Windows 1.0 launch are so good. Steve: But no, that's the sales side. I actually managed the engineers because the guy who was doing it wasn't being successful, and we had to ship the thing.

claims.claim: The speaker describes how Microsoft was trying to keep with OS/2, and that Bill Gates was very frustrated with IBM, while the speaker knew his job was to ride the bear.
claims.quote: We're trying to keep with OS/2, Bill's very frustrated with IBM. I'm frustrated, but I know my job is to ride the bear. Bill's pushing Windows hard, but we still suspected OS/2 could be the winner because it came from IBM.

claims.claim: Steve Ballmer believes he should hold Microsoft stock due to loyalty and emotional detachment, despite the possibility of underperformance, as the dividend checks and other assets fund his philanthropy.
claims.quote: I said, look. My loyalty trumps my emotional attachment. I can get through my emotional attachment, but my loyalty. And look. I think of the thing as like a two-headed hydra. I thought about this the whole way. Things could go to nothing or things could explode.

claims.claim: Ballmer states that he does not need to sell Microsoft stock because he has enough money to live on and the dividend checks plus other assets fund his philanthropy.
claims.quote: I don’t need the money. I got plenty to live on without selling anything. That’s number one. Financially, where’s that money going to go? Some will go to my kids, but most of it’s going to go to the government or to philanthropy. Why would I sell, so we have less to give to philanthropy someday, unless I really think Microsoft’s going to underperform the market by essentially the capital gains rat

claims.claim: Ballmer mentions that the dividend checks from Microsoft and other assets are close to what he gives away to philanthropy, allowing him to fund philanthropy without selling additional shares.
claims.quote: Between Microsoft and the other stuff I own, the dividend checks are pretty close to what we give away. You can look at the appreciation, but we’re just above the dividend checks now.

claims.claim: Ballmer notes that he holds mostly index funds outside of Microsoft, with some money in Stagwell Media, but mostly in index funds.
claims.quote: I have one business I invested in with a guy who I went to college with who worked at Microsoft. It’s called Stagwell Media. It’s a marketing services company. Call it a modern day ad agency, but it’s not really an ad agency. A guy named Mark Penn. I do have some money that’s not in index funds, but mostly I’m in index funds.

claims.claim: Steve Ballmer explains why he held onto his Microsoft stock despite his partners selling, citing loyalty and a desire to give money to philanthropy rather than pay capital gains taxes.
claims.quote: I don’t need the money. I got plenty to live on without selling anything. That’s number one. Financially, where’s that money going to go? Some will go to my kids, but most of it’s going to go to the government or to philanthropy. claims.claim: Steve Ballmer states that Microsoft stock can go to zero, but his family and he can still live, and he is okay with any outcome.
claims.quote: What’s the worst thing that happens? Microsoft goes to zero? Probably not, but even if Microsoft goes to zero, me and my family, we can live, we can give away money, it’s not going to go to zero. And I’m okay any way it goes. I’m fine.

claims.claim: Steve Ballmer compares the security of his Clippers and Intuit Dome assets to Microsoft, stating that unlike Microsoft, his assets cannot go to zero and are far more secure.
claims.quote: Now, that I do not own the financial purposes. And I will also tell you, unlike Microsoft, it cannot go to zero. David: Like the asset value? Steve: Not a chance. It is far more secure than Microsoft. Why? David: Not making more of them.

claims.claim: Steve Ballmer contrasts the career mobility in sports versus Microsoft, noting that in Microsoft he could always find a job for someone, whereas in sports there are only 30 head coaching jobs.
claims.quote: Again, not what we want, but the reality is we don’t want people held back in their career. It’s not like Microsoft where I felt like I could always find a job that somebody should want. That’s different.

claims.claim: Steve Ballmer explains that in Microsoft, the domain is growing, and they can move people to work on different products, unlike sports where career moves are limited.
claims.quote: David: Microsoft, your domain is always growing. Steve: The domain is growing, or number of people, you can move people. Oh, you’re an engineer. You’re bored. You’ve worked on X. We’ll move you to work on a different product, for example. It’s different the way you think about people, primarily because of the union, but also there are only 30 head coaching jobs.
